independentCheck.printedAnswerStatus: 200 J follows only from reinterpretation of the specified low-temperature absorption as 600 J absorbed at the hot reservoir; NOT derivable as stated for a positive-work Carnot engine

items.reviewReason: Original printed p.153 explicitly says the Carnot engine absorbs 600 J of heat at the low temperature of 400 K, although the high-temperature reservoir is 600 K. Using 600 J as high-side input changes the source meaning and gives 200 J, the publisher answer. In a reversed Carnot refrigerator absorbing 600 J from 400 K, the input work would instead be 300 J. If 600 J were heat rejected to 400 K from an engine, its reversible work would also be 300 J. These are distinct devices and transfers; preserve the publisher conflict rather than relabel the source as correct.
items.classification: compulsory source contradiction; block unique assessed answer
items.independentVariantRequirement: Explicitly say reversible Carnot engine absorbs 600 J from the 600 K hot reservoir and rejects heat to the 400 K sink; retain publisher original unchanged.

independentCheck.printedAnswerStatus: 198 s is reproduced using c≈4186 J/(kg·K); standard rounded c=4200 gives 198.6 s (about 199 s to nearest whole second), a minor constant/rounding difference

items.reviewReason: Original p.153 gives 220 W, 136 g water, initial 23.5 °C, and asks time to bring it to the boiling point while ignoring heat loss. It does not supply the numerical value of specific heat capacity. Assuming ordinary water boils at 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure gives ΔT=76.5 K; with c=4186 J/(kg K), t≈197.96 s and printed 198 s. With c=4200, t≈198.62 s, a one-second rounded difference. Do not confuse bringing water to its boiling point with vaporizing it, which would require latent heat.

independentCheck.printedAnswerStatus: 397 K agrees under Carnot, fixed sink and room temperature 298 K; 300 K would give 400 K, so source alone does not uniquely fix the printed numeric answer

items.reviewReason: The source says 'a heat engine at room temperature' has 50% efficiency and asks the difference between two heat source temperatures after efficiency becomes 70%. It does not numerically define room temperature and does not explicitly name an ideal reversible Carnot engine with a fixed cold reservoir. The Carnot formula η=1−T_C/T_H at the same cold temperature implies ΔT_H=(4/3)T_C, yielding ≈397.33 K if T_C=298 K, consistent with its 397 K printed result. At T_C=300 K the same formula gives 400 K, so the printed answer is assumption-specific, not an unqualified general result.
items.classification: compulsory Carnot/fixed sink/room temperature assumptions; compulsory SLO cognitive review
